extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, physicians/surgeons, astronomers, and antiquaries (17th-century scientific readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Reporting and interpreting empirical observations and practical procedures across domains (magnetism, medical practice, architecture, and astronomy), including measurement methods, procedural steps, and rules for inferring causes and timings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for calculating magnetic variation
rubrics_metrics.description: To calculate exactly the magnetic variation at any place requires a great many observations made at the same time, not at sea but ashore, with greater care and attention than the generality of sailors apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author warns that many contemporaneous, carefully made terrestrial observations are requisite; further, the proportion in which attractive power decreases with distance from a magnet is undetermined (making calculation futile until known), and secular changes in variation mean centuries of data may be required to establish a complete doctrine of the magnetical system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and inference about magnetical-pole motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed changes in compass variation imply magnetical poles may move, but such motion is not necessarily a rotation about the Earth's axis; patterns of variation across latitudes and longitudes must be compared to decide motion type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparative observations across parallels/longitudes: if variation changed only in longitude in the same latitude, that would indicate rotation about the axis; the contrary (observed non-uniform changes) argues against simple axial rotation. The author emphasizes careful geographic comparison to infer pole motion and cautions many unknowns (whether poles move together, equally, circularly or libratorily).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation of moxa for cautery
rubrics_metrics.description: The plant is dried in the shade, freed from filth and harder stalks, rubbed between the hands till it becomes like cotton, formed into a little cone (about the bulk of a pea) or a paper-rolled cylinder divided into pellets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical preparation steps are given verbatim (shade-drying, cleaning, rubbing to cotton-like consistency, shaping into cones/pellets). The pellet apex is lit, base placed next to skin; a little blister is raised and eschar management (garlic applied for 24 hours, plantain leaf sides for opening/healing) is prescribed. Many repeated burns (sometimes up to 50 pellets) are noted as practiced in Japan; also recommended is inventing gentler cauteries than bare fire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moxa application sites and indications
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice of burn points is essential: different illnesses require burning at specific locations (e.g., linea alba avoided as it causes barrenness; above the navel restores appetite; shoulder blades for appetite; loins/os sacrum for gonorrhea and spermatic weakness; abdomen for colic; chin for toothache; four points near os sacrum for grievous chronic cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author stresses that the 'whole art lies in designing the points to be burnt for each distemper' and that particular surgeons keep rules and images marking proper places. Examples and cautions (e.g., avoiding linea alba) are provided as prescriptive practice guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acupuncture instrument and insertion protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: Needles are long, slender, sharp, of gold or silver, with a wreathed handle; conveyed by hand or a little mallet into the part, a finger's breadth or more, held there for the space of 30 breathings if tolerable; otherwise repeat punctures are used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Further procedural rules: puncture when the patient is fasting; deeper in greater disease, older men, grown persons, and in fleshy parts; used chiefly for head and lower belly ailments; apply to the part whence the distemper arises; use pulse to find points; surgeons keep images showing the places. An eyewitness case (soldier puncturing four pyloric-region points) is cited as example of rapid relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surgical cautery practice and cautions
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent and properly located cauteries (burning) are used for chronic diseases; particular places are avoided because of harmful effects (e.g., burning on linea alba causes barrenness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text recommends caution in site selection and documents traditional rules/images used by practitioners; it also notes cultural differences in acceptance (Japanese preference) and suggests invention of gentler cauteries is desirable to reduce harshness while preserving efficacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiognomy as a diagnostic/character analytic method
rubrics_metrics.description: The countenance is the epitome of the whole man, representing inward passions and motions of the soul; temperament of the body influences lineaments, complexion, features, and air of the face, allowing signs of dispositions and virtues/vices to be read from facial differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author provides general rules: differentiate choleric, phlegmatic, sanguine, melancholic dispositions, discuss effects of climate, custom, and dissimulation, and list signs per nation/temperament. These are presented as a scheme of physiognomy for diagnosis/character reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural analysis: masonry courses, bonding, and proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: Roman wall observed to be faced with small square stone in level courses (about 4 inches thick), with interleaved courses of Roman brick (lateres Diatoni) laid lengthwise and endwise, serving as throughs to bind the sides; wall middle filled with mortar and pebble; note uniformity and proportion in courses as essential to beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: record course counts (e.g., 20 courses small stone, 5 courses Roman brick, etc.), measure brick dimensions (here ~17" × 11" × 2.5"), note the absence of casements/loop-holes, compare to classical sources (Vitruvius, Pliny) to test measures, and judge proportion/uniformity as contributors to aesthetic and structural qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roman brick dimensions as evidential measure
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed Roman bricks are about 17 inches in length, about 11 inches broad, and 2½ inches thick, compatible with Pliny's measures and informative about ancient standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use measured brick dimensions to adjudicate between variant classical authorities (Pliny vs Vitruvius) and to reason about building practice (smaller bricks giving greater firmness via greater number of angles). Measurements are used as empirical evidence to correct textual sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards and procedures for observing planetary conjunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure distances between planets (centres, near limbs, remote limbs) with a micrometer and long telescope (here a 16-foot glass); measure distances to fixed stars with a sextant; repeat measures and record times; use ephemerides and assumed latitudes to compute true longitudes and latitudinal differences and hence determine conjunction times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed procedural notes: take repeated measures (and note repeats), use both micrometer/telescope and sextant for cross-checks, reference distances to known stars (e.g., Castor's heel, Lion's heart), correct observational measures by assumed latitudes from tables, compute apparent motions and use proportional interpolation (motion per hours/days) to find the true conjunction time, and account for instrument/error sources (wind shaking the sextant, observer illness, use of assistants). Examples of the full calculation process and numerous recorded measures are provided as templates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational measurement protocol and error handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Take multiple repeated observations, use appropriate instruments for the quantity measured, have assistants when necessary, and note environmental/instrumental conditions that affect precision (e.g., wind shaking the sextant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author repeatedly records repeats of the same measure, uses different instruments (micrometer with long glass vs sextant), acknowledges limitations (dubious measures when wind interfered), and adjusts confidence accordingly (considers differences less than half a minute inconsequential). Use of assistants when ill is documented and recommended for continuity of observation.
